analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 15 Democratic cosponsors in March 2015, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal bankruptcy law treats student loans like almost nothing else: you cannot erase them in bankruptcy unless you can prove repaying them is an 'undue hardship' — a standard so tough that most debtors never even try. This bill would change that for privately issued student loans only, letting people who have fallen into genuine financial ruin discharge private loans the way they can discharge credit card debt or medical bills. Government-backed student loans would keep the stricter rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers whose finances collapsed under privately issued student loans. These loans typically carry higher interest rates and fewer repayment protections than federal loans, yet today they are nearly impossible to discharge. Under the bill, a borrower in bankruptcy court who meets the normal bankruptcy standards could erase them, giving a fresh start to people who are otherwise stuck with the debt for life.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Distressed borrowers with private student loans

how_it_helps.text: Amends the federal bankruptcy code (section 523(a)(8)) so that privately issued student loans are treated like other consumer debt and can be discharged in bankruptcy.
Leaves the special 'undue hardship' rule in place only for loans made, insured, or guaranteed by a government or government-funded program, so the change targets private lenders.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan companies, which would face the real possibility that troubled borrowers legally erase their debt. That risk would also likely show up in lending: private lenders could charge higher rates, lend more cautiously, or require cosigners more often. Taxpayers are not directly on the hook, because government-backed loans keep their current treatment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student loan companies and future borrowers

drawbacks.text: Easier discharge of private loans could raise the cost or reduce the availability of private student loans for everyone, since lenders would price in the added bankruptcy risk.

The relief reaches only borrowers already in severe financial distress who file bankruptcy; it does nothing to lower tuition, interest rates, or monthly payments for the far larger group of borrowers who stay current.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people this bill targets — borrowers already in bankruptcy with private loans — the benefit is large and concrete: a chance to escape lifelong debt. The cost falls on private lenders and, indirectly, on future private-loan borrowers through somewhat higher rates. That trade-off mirrors the one Congress already accepted for every other kind of consumer debt, which is the core argument supporters made.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2015 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or brought it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 12, 2015, joined by 15 Democratic cosponsors including Senators Warren, Franken, and Gillibrand.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; that referral was the bill's last action of record.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action ever occurred, and the bill expired with the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan companies keep the protection that lets them pursue borrowers for life, because nothing changed. Borrowers drowning in private student debt gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private student lenders, whose loans stay nearly undischargeable

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to let private student loans be discharged in bankruptcy.

for.name: 15 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it all-Democratic support with no Republican signers.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to expire at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the two years it sat in the panel.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Today their loans are nearly impossible to discharge, so lenders can pursue struggling borrowers for decades. The bill would remove that shield, exposing them to the same bankruptcy risk as other consumer lenders; their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against borrowers seeking relief.
